brief_item.title: CodeGrep：14B RL检索器压缩代码Agent探索开销
brief_item.core_conclusion: 代码Agent的token多耗在找文件而非写补丁，把一个14B RL检索器注入冻结下游Agent后探索开销明显压缩，解决率基本守住。
brief_item.mechanism: GRPO训练的14B检索器每轮最多8个并行只读工具调用，把候选文件清单注入冻结下游Agent提示。
brief_item.result: 500实例上解决率由25.8%升至27.0%，已解决轮数和token分别降约15%与19%。
brief_item.boundary: 解决率仅升1.2pp且归因模糊，第897步早停，仅刻画一种下游。
brief_item.project_relevance: 检索器文件精度需越过约0.68才降本，低于0.45反拖累Agent，可作精度基线。

facts.title: CodeGrep: An RL-Trained Retrieval Agent for LLM Coding Agents
facts.event_hint: CodeGrep: a 14B agent-style code retriever trained end-to-end with GRPO and injected into a frozen OpenHands agent on SWE-Bench Verified to cut exploration rounds and tokens.
facts.problem: Modern LLM coding agents (Claude Code, OpenHands) spend most of their token budget finding the file to patch rather than writing the patch. A 30B OpenHands agent on SWE-Bench Verified averages 23 rounds and 631K tokens per resolved issue, dominated by grep, glob and view_file calls in ambiguous exploration loops, often 20+ rounds in a wrong direction before giving up. Whether a specialized retrieval submodule can shorten this exploration phase (H2: same issues resolved with shorter rollout) without hurting resolve (H1: better retrieval raises resolve) had not been jointly tested in the open.
facts.mechanism: CodeGrep is a 14B retriever built on Qwen3-14B-Instruct, trained end-to-end with GRPO (on ms-swift, LoRA + optimizer offload + vLLM-colocated rollout on a single 8xB200 node, ~27h wall-clock, early-stopped at step 897 of 2000). It exposes three read-only primitives (grep regex search, glob path matching, read file contents) and emits up to 8 parallel tool calls per turn executed concurrently inside a Git-worktree RL environment, capped at 4 turns (3 exploration + 1 answer), max 32 tool execs per rollout. Supervision is mined from 67K open-source OpenHands trajectories via CATM (one-to-many attribution), giving 31,977 effective training samples (47.7% retention) judged by GLM-5.1-FP8 (16-way parallel, ~5h). At inference, CodeGrep takes the issue description, emits a candidate-file list injected into the prompt of a frozen downstream OpenHands agent (Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507) — only the retriever is trained, so downstream effects attribute cleanly. Reward-design study v1->v2->v3 shows moving the efficiency signal from the reward layer to the advantage layer holds KL drift to ~0.09-0.15 vs v1's ~0.31, and v3 drops an auxiliary line-range term absent from the downstream editor.

evidence.claim: Injected into a frozen OpenHands agent on all 500 SWE-Bench Verified instances, CodeGrep v3 lifts resolve rate by +1.2pp (25.8% -> 27.0%) while cutting resolved rounds 23.0 -> 19.6 (-15%) and resolved tokens 631K -> 514K (-19%); on unresolved instances it also lowers rounds from 32.0 to 27.5.
evidence.value: +1.2pp resolve (25.8%->27.0%); -15% resolved rounds; -19% resolved tokens; unresolved rounds 32.0->27.5
evidence.baseline: no-retrieval baseline (OpenHands Qwen3-30B-A3B, 25.8% resolve at 23.0 resolved rounds / 631K resolved tokens / 32.0 unresolved rounds)
evidence.condition: SWE-Bench Verified, 500 instances, frozen OpenHands + Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 at temp 0, 100-round max
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 7 (Section 4.3 Table 3, full efficiency columns incl. Unresolved r.)

evidence.claim: Section 5.3 pooled-vs-paired control: the Table 3 efficiency numbers are pooled over each config's own resolved set (baseline 129, v3 135 instances), mixing a genuine efficiency effect with a selection effect. Restricted to the 96 instances both configurations resolve, rounds fall 20.1 -> 18.3 (-9%) and tokens 525K -> 448K (-15%), preserving 60-80% of the pooled effect and confirming the improvement as per-issue acceleration rather than only a selection artifact.
evidence.value: paired-instance: -9% rounds (20.1->18.3); -15% tokens (525K->448K); 60-80% of pooled effect retained
evidence.baseline: no-retrieval baseline on the 96 paired-resolved instances
evidence.condition: 96 instances resolved by both baseline and CodeGrep v3
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 8 (Section 5.3 Pooled vs. paired-instance efficiency)

evidence.claim: Across three retrievers, downstream utility follows a precision threshold with three regimes: BM25 at file-precision 0.375 degrades the agent (resolve 25.2%, resolved tokens 763K, +21% vs baseline); Jina-1.5B at precision 0.445 is neutral (resolve 25.8%, resolved tokens 587K, -7%); CodeGrep at precision 0.677 crosses the threshold. The neutral-to-net-positive transition lies between precision 0.45 and 0.68.
evidence.value: BM25 0.375 hurts; Jina 0.445 neutral; CodeGrep 0.677 buys efficiency; transition in (0.45, 0.68)
evidence.condition: SWE-Bench Verified, frozen OpenHands agent; file-precision on internal eval set
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 7 (Section 5.1 precision threshold, Takeaway; Table 3)

evidence.claim: Reward-design study: applying the tool-call efficiency signal at the advantage layer (v2/v3) instead of multiplicative reward-layer scaling (v1) reduces KL-to-reference drift from ~0.31 to ~0.09/0.15; v3 stabilizes average rollout turns at ~2.1 (from v1's ~3.8, 1.65x). v1 matches v3's 27.0% resolve but delivers only -1.3% rounds / -0.6% tokens vs baseline, whereas v3 delivers -15% / -19%.
evidence.value: KL 0.31 -> 0.09/0.15; v1 inference 3.8 turns vs v3 2.3; v1 -1.3% rounds/-0.6% tokens vs v3 -15%/-19%
evidence.condition: GRPO training of CodeGrep, ~900-step run
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 7 (Section 5.2 Reward iterations: three failure modes)

evidence.claim: Action-level case study (django-15278): without a retrieval hint the frozen agent stalls after 74 actions and 3.2M tokens with no passing patch; with CodeGrep injection the same agent succeeds in 15 actions and 307K tokens (~10x fewer tokens), locating the fix in related.py. CodeGrep does not supply the fix — it compresses the exploratory prefix the agent otherwise burns on repo-wide find/grep sweeps for issue-prose tokens absent from the codebase.
evidence.value: 74 actions / 3.2M tokens (stall) -> 15 actions / 307K tokens (pass); ~10x token reduction
evidence.condition: single representative issue, frozen OpenHands + Qwen3-30B-A3B, action-level trace
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 8 (Section 6 Case Study: Where the Token Savings Come From)

facts.evaluation_context: Benchmark: SWE-Bench Verified (500 instances). Downstream agent: OpenHands with Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 at temperature 0, 100-round max, frozen. Baseline reproduces public reference: 25.8% resolve at 23.0 resolved rounds / 631K resolved tokens / 32.0 unresolved rounds (within 1 SD of publicly reported 25.2 +/- 0.7%). Six configs compared: baseline, BM25, Jina-1.5B, CodeGrep v1/v2/v3 (Table 3 reports Resolve, Resolved r., Resolved tok., Unresolved r.). Training: GRPO on ms-swift, LoRA + optimizer offload + vLLM-colocated rollout, single 8xB200 node, ~27h wall-clock, early-stop step 897 of planned 2000. RL environment: Git-worktree per rollout, max 8 parallel tools per turn, max 32 tool execs per rollout. Data: 67,074 raw trajectories -> 31,977 effective training samples (47.7% retention) judged by GLM-5.1-FP8. Efficiency accounting: Table 3 columns are pooled over each config's own resolved/unresolved set; paired-instance control (n=96) in Section 5.3.
facts.limitations: Resolve-rate lift is small (+1.2pp, 25.8%->27.0%) and CodeGrep v1 reaches the same 27.0% resolve without the efficiency gain, so the resolve contribution is not clearly attributable to v3 specifically; v3's marginal quality gain over v2 (median F-beta +28%) yields only +0.4pp resolve, the rest absorbed as rollout compression — consistent with file localization not being the binding bottleneck on resolve rate. Training is single-node, early-stopped at step 897 of a 2000-step budget, so full-budget behavior is unknown. Downstream utility is characterized only for OpenHands + Qwen3-30B-A3B; the precision-threshold transferability to other downstream agents is explicitly left open (Section 7). Closed commercial comparator Cognition SWE-grep has an undisclosed reward formulation (Table 6 marks components n/s), so component-level comparison is partial. Model release is promised ('we will release') but not yet public at paper time. Section 5.3 confirms the pooled efficiency numbers mix a selection effect with a genuine effect, but the paired-instance control (-9% rounds / -15% tokens on 96 shared-resolve instances) preserves 60-80% of the pooled magnitude, so the dividend is real per-issue acceleration, not only selection.
facts.project_relevance: Directly on-topic for the agent-acceleration card's central question of reducing repeated Read/Grep/Glob and shortening the exploration phase: CodeGrep is a concrete, open, RL-trained retrieval submodule that delivers a measured -15% resolved rounds / -19% resolved tokens efficiency dividend on a real SWE-Bench Verified workload while preserving resolve, confirmed as per-issue acceleration (not only a selection artifact) by the paired-instance control in Section 5.3. The action-level case study (74 actions/3.2M tokens -> 15 actions/307K tokens) pinpoints the token savings to the exploratory prefix of repo-wide find/grep sweeps. The precision-threshold characterization (BM25 0.375 hurts, Jina 0.445 neutral, CodeGrep 0.677 buys efficiency; transition in 0.45-0.68) is project-actionable: it gives a concrete precision bar a code retriever must clear before it reduces rollout cost, and warns that naive lexical retrieval actively harms efficiency. The advantage-layer vs reward-layer RL finding is a reusable design rule for training future tool-using retrieval agents.

brief_item.title: SAC：CXL缓存行粒度共享支撑稀疏注意力解耦KV缓存
brief_item.core_conclusion: 稀疏注意力模型的解耦KV缓存靠RDMA整块拉取，浪费带宽与本地内存，换成CXL缓存行粒度共享后端到端时延与吞吐同时改善。
brief_item.mechanism: CXL Type-3设备暴露缓存行粒度读写，解码实例按层算top-k后按需从CXL池取热KV入显存。
brief_item.result: 8卡H20加2TB CXL池上吞吐约2.1倍，TTFT与TBT分别降至约九分之一与二分之一。
brief_item.boundary: 未说明CXL是真实3.0硬件还是模拟器，绝对时延未公开。
brief_item.project_relevance: 缓存行粒度内存语义的收益能传导到推理指标，需先确认CXL介质真实性再纳入池化方案。

facts.title: SAC: Disaggregated KV Cache System for Sparse Attention LLMs with CXL
facts.event_hint: SAC (Sparse Attention on CXL): first CXL-based disaggregated KV cache system for sparse attention LLM serving (DeepSeek-V3.2 AWQ 4-bit on SGLang/HiSparse, 8-H20 GPU server with 2TB CXL memory pool).
facts.problem: Traditional RDMA-based disaggregated KV cache pools (e.g., MoonCake, LMCache) full-fetch the entire prefix KV cache from remote to local memory before decoding. For sparse attention models (DeepSeek Sparse Attention, top-k=2048 per layer), only a small fraction of KV entries are active per layer, so full-fetching wastes transmission bandwidth (transmission bottleneck P1: long queuing delays and degraded TTFT/throughput at high client concurrency on 100 Gbps RNIC) and wastes local memory (P2: only 21% of KV cache utilized at 128K context; DeepSeek-V3.2 needs 9.2 GB/request at 128K, requiring TB-level local memory for high concurrency). RDMA's message-based send/recv semantics also impose per-request software-stack overhead that accumulates across all attention layers for fine-grained top-k reads, and during decode the RDMA path contends with the HiSparse swap-in process for PCIe bandwidth, raising TBT.
facts.mechanism: SAC replaces RDMA with a CXL-based disaggregated KV cache pool exposing hardware-managed load/store semantics at cache-line granularity, accessed through a CXL switch (CXL 2.0/3.0, Type-3 memory devices). Built on the HiSparse framework inside SGLang, the decode instance computes top-k indices per attention layer at runtime and uses an optimized Swap-in CUDA kernel (miss identification + LRU eviction + page-table update + fetch) to fetch only the required top-k KV entries directly from the CXL memory pool into GPU HBM on demand; newly generated token KV is written back to CXL. The CXL system maps all KV data into a global CXL address space shared across compute instances, with device initialization, optimized read/write kernels, and device interleaving across multiple CXL memory devices (interleaving mitigates link-level contention and is shown to scale toward the local-DRAM bound). Prefill instance writes full KV blocks to the CXL pool after prefill. The HiSparse device_buffer_size (hot KV kept in GPU HBM) is a key tunable; a 6K buffer yields ~10.4% higher average throughput than a 4K buffer by lowering the KV miss rate.

evidence.claim: On DeepSeek-V3.2 (AWQ 4-bit) end-to-end serving via SGLang/HiSparse on an 8-H20 GPU server with a 2TB CXL memory pool, across context lengths 16K-128K (ShareGPT, 512 requests, 1K-token output, concurrency 64 in the decode/Cache-Hit round), SAC achieves on average 2.1x higher throughput, 9.7x lower TTFT and 1.8x lower TBT compared with an RDMA-based memory pool baseline.
evidence.value: 2.1x throughput; 9.7x lower TTFT; 1.8x lower TBT (Round-2 decode averages, 16K-128K context)
evidence.condition: DeepSeek-V3.2 AWQ 4-bit on SGLang/HiSparse, 8x H20 GPU, 2TB CXL pool, ShareGPT 512 requests, 1K output, Round-2 concurrency 64, context 16K-128K
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 7 (Section 5, 5.1 End-to-End Performance Comparison, Figures 9-10)

evidence.claim: Across both prefill (Round-1) and decode (Round-2) rounds, SAC throughput stays within 91% of the local-DRAM upper bound with only marginal TBT/TTFT increase, i.e., about a 9% throughput degradation versus the non-disaggregated local-memory baseline.
evidence.value: ~9% throughput degradation vs local DRAM upper bound (throughput within 91% of DRAM)
evidence.condition: DeepSeek-V3.2 AWQ 4-bit on SGLang/HiSparse, 8x H20 GPU, 2TB CXL pool, 16K-128K context, both rounds
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 7 (Section 5.1, narrative following Figures 9-10)

evidence.claim: The 1.8x TBT penalty of the RDMA baseline relative to SAC is attributed to severe PCIe bus contention, since the PCIe bus must simultaneously handle incoming KV cache traffic and the HiSparse swap-in process; the 9.7x TTFT penalty is attributed to high client concurrency saturating transmission bandwidth during KV retrieval and increasing queuing delays.
evidence.value: RDMA TBT 1.8x vs SAC (PCIe contention); RDMA TTFT 9.7x vs SAC (transmission bandwidth saturation under concurrency)
evidence.condition: Round-2 decode, DeepSeek-V3.2 on SGLang/HiSparse
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 7 (Section 5.1, explanation of Round-2 results)

evidence.claim: For DeepSeek-V3.2 serving 128K-context ShareGPT requests with 1K-token output, only 21% of the KV cache is actually utilized during decoding while the per-request KV footprint is 9.2 GB.
evidence.value: 21% KV utilization at 128K context; 9.2 GB KV per request at 128K
evidence.baseline: full prefix KV cache fetched locally
evidence.condition: DeepSeek-V3.2, ShareGPT dataset, 1K-token output, 128K context
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 4 (Figure 4, Section 3.1 P2: Local Memory Wasting)

evidence.claim: Scaling the HiSparse GPU device buffer from 4K to 6K reduces the KV cache miss rate and yields an average throughput 10.4% higher, while interleaving KV cache storage across multiple CXL devices mitigates link-level contention and is projected to further close the gap to the local-DRAM baseline.
evidence.value: 6K buffer: +10.4% avg throughput vs 4K; device interleaving mitigates link contention
evidence.condition: DeepSeek-V3.2 on SGLang/HiSparse, 16K-128K context
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 9 (Section 5.4/5.5, Figures 13-14)

facts.evaluation_context: Workload: DeepSeek-V3.2 (AWQ 4-bit quantization) end-to-end LLM serving integrated into SGLang and the HiSparse framework, context lengths 16K-128K, ShareGPT dataset (512 requests, 1K-token output). A two-round setup isolates stages: Round-1 Cache Populate (prefill instance) at concurrency 8, Round-2 Cache Hit (decode instance, prefill bypassed) at concurrency 64. Hardware topology: 8x H20 GPU server plus a 2TB CXL memory pool as KV cache backend (CXL 2.0/3.0 Type-3, cache-line-granularity load/store via CXL switch). Baselines: RDMA-based disaggregated memory pool and local host DRAM as non-disaggregated upper bound. Absolute throughput axes: Round-1 0-150 tok/s, Round-2 0-1200 tok/s; TBT axes 0-75 ms (R1) / 0-200 ms (R2); TTFT axes 0-240 s (R1) / 0-40 s (R2).
facts.limitations: The supplement confirms the hardware setup (8x H20, 2TB CXL pool), concurrency (8 prefill / 64 decode), ShareGPT 512-request workload, and the 91%-of-DRAM throughput figure, and attributes the RDMA TBT/TTFT penalties to PCIe bus contention and transmission-bandwidth saturation respectively. However, exact absolute per-context throughput/TTFT/TBT values behind the 2.1x/9.7x/1.8x ratios are only available as figure axis ranges, not per-data-point numbers. The supplement still does not explicitly state whether the CXL fabric is CXL 3.0 hardware versus an emulator/simulator, nor the exact CXL device count (only the aggregate 2TB pool) or per-device capacity. Energy, cost-per-token and CPU utilization impact remain unquantified.
facts.project_relevance: Directly on-topic for the memory-semantics/DSA card: SAC is a concrete case of changing the memory sharing/placement/remote-access semantics (CXL cache-line-granularity load/store replacing RDMA message semantics) and demonstrates that the fine-grained memory-semantic advantage propagates to end-to-end LLM serving throughput/TTFT/TBT for a real sparse-attention model on production-class H20 hardware. The PCIe-contention root cause for RDMA TBT and the bandwidth-saturation root cause for TTFT validate the project's question of whether micro-level memory-semantic gains conduct to end-to-end AI data-path metrics. Residual verification gap: confirm whether the CXL fabric is emulated and obtain per-context absolute latency/concurrency/CPU-utilization numbers before claiming a deployable win beyond the reported ratios.

evidence_gaps.question: Is the CXL memory pool real CXL 3.0 hardware or an emulator/simulator, and what are the absolute CXL/DRAM/RDMA read latencies (microseconds) behind the Figure 5 relative multiples?
What exact GPU model, concurrency level, batch size, and CXL device count/capacity were used for the 2.1x/9.7x/1.8x end-to-end comparison, and what are the absolute throughput, TTFT and TBT values?

facts.title: Code Isn't Memory: A Structural Codebase Index Inside a Coding Agent
facts.event_hint: First leak-audited, model-controlled causal ablation of a structural codebase index (codebase_search + codebase_graph) inside the SuperCoder open-source coding-agent harness, on SWE-PolyBench Verified and SWE-bench Pro.
facts.problem: Coding-agent retrieval implementations vary widely (agentic grep, file-dependency repo maps, semantic/graph search, structural codebase indices), but the field has no clean causal answer to whether adding a structural codebase index actually changes resolve or cost. Prior work either compares whole harnesses (where retrieval is confounded with prompt, tool surface and control loop) or evaluates retrieval components in isolation against acc@k without the downstream agentic loop that turns ranking into a fix. Whether 'grep is all you need' for code tasks (where the candidate beyond grep is a structural index combining semantic + lexical + call-graph) was unanswered.
facts.mechanism: SuperCoder harness exposes two first-class engine tools, codebase_search and codebase_graph, as a structural codebase index (semantic + lexical + call-graph) built once per repository. The causal ablation toggles only these two tools off to form SC-OFF while keeping model, prompts, sandbox, scorer, seeds, 30-min wall-clock cap and the rest of the toolset identical. A cross-harness comparator (OpenCode, an independent harness whose retrieval is built around ripgrep and file reads with no structural index) tests reproducibility. Localization is measured under a dual-view extractor: View A counts every path the agent saw (including engine result lists); View B (agent-targeted, adopted as primary) strips paths whose only provenance is an engine result list while keeping the engine's natural-language query arguments, applied uniformly so it is a strict no-op for SC-OFF/OpenCode (which emit no engine calls). Artifacts released: per-cell exclusion ledger, leak-audit script, dual-view localization extractor, full results database.

evidence.claim: Within-harness ablation: toggling the structural index on (SC-ON) moves View B acc@5 localization from 44.3% to 84.5% (paired Wilcoxon on per-instance pass@1, n=80, p<0.0001), a +39.6pp gain.
evidence.baseline: SC-OFF (same harness, codebase_search and codebase_graph removed)
evidence.condition: View B localization, Claude Opus 4.7, SWE-PolyBench Verified + SWE-bench Pro, 3 seeds, paired Wilcoxon, pairwise n=80 (SC-ON vs SC-OFF)
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 7-8 (Section 6.2 Table V; Section 7 Discussion)

evidence.claim: Within-harness ablation: resolve moves from 41.9% (SC-OFF) to 50.4% (SC-ON), a +7.9pp gain (paired Wilcoxon n=80, p=0.003), consistent across all three seeds (per-seed SC-ON 48.8/53.6/48.8; SC-OFF 43.9/41.5/40.2).
evidence.condition: resolve metric (F2P pass and P2P pass), Claude Opus 4.7, SWE-PolyBench Verified + SWE-bench Pro, 3 seeds, n=80
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 7 (Section 6.1-6.2, Table III and Table V)

evidence.claim: Headline cost/effort magnitudes (mean of seed means, per-cell on legit cells): $/solved is $2.30 (SC-ON) vs $2.84 (SC-OFF) vs $2.92 (OpenCode); $/cell mean is $1.15 vs $1.19 vs $1.32 (SC-ON vs SC-OFF paired Wilcoxon p=0.73, statistically null); mean turns 28.3 vs 36.2 vs 36.0 (SC-ON vs SC-OFF p<0.0001); mean tokens 10.1k vs 11.1k vs 14.0k (SC-ON vs SC-OFF p=0.027); mean wall-clock 4.5 vs 5.5 vs 5.4 min. The $/solved gap is driven by SC-ON's higher resolve rate at near-equal per-cell spend, not by cheaper per-cell cost.
evidence.condition: per-cell cost_usd from unified provider gateway, 3 seeds, Claude Opus 4.7, paired Wilcoxon
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 7 (Section 6.1 Table IV, 6.2 Table V, Fig. 2)

evidence.claim: Cross-harness check: SC-ON resolves 50.4% vs OpenCode 45.3% (paired Wilcoxon n=78, p=0.087, not at conventional significance) and View B acc@5 84.5% vs 75.3% (p=0.080); direction is consistent across all three seeds but marginal. SC-ON's $/solved is ~21% lower than OpenCode's ($2.30 vs $2.92) and per-cell cost is statistically null (p=0.35).
evidence.value: resolve p=0.087 (+6.0pp); acc@5 p=0.080 (+8.1pp); $/solved ~21% lower (marginal, not significant)
evidence.condition: Claude Opus 4.7, 3 seeds, pairwise n=78 (SC-ON vs OpenCode)
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 7 (Section 6.1 Cross-harness comparison, Table IV)

evidence.claim: Where the index helps most (exploratory, no significance claims): by gold-file count the within-harness acc@5 gap is largest in the 3+ file bucket (91.3% ON vs 44.9% OFF, +46.4pp), consistent with the call-graph intuition; by language the localization gain is largest in Go (95.4% vs 44.8%) and Python (82.9% vs 42.4%), more modest in Java (71.7% vs 46.7%). Rank-1 first-gold placement is 77.4% (SC-ON) vs 33.3% (SC-OFF).
evidence.value: 3+ file bucket acc@5 +46.4pp; Go +50.6pp; Python +40.5pp; rank-1 gold 77.4% vs 33.3%
evidence.condition: exploratory slices, per-language n=18-46, per-file-count n=46/18/27, View B acc@5
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 8 (Section 6.3 Fig. 3-4, Table VI)

facts.evaluation_context: Three arms on the same instance set: SC-ON (SuperCoder with codebase_search + codebase_graph), SC-OFF (same harness with those two tools removed), OpenCode (independent ripgrep+file-read harness). Model held fixed: Claude Opus 4.7 across 3 seeds, pass@1 per seed. Benchmarks: SWE-PolyBench Verified (Go, Java, Python) + SWE-bench Pro (longer-context Python); 91 instances total; JavaScript/TypeScript not covered. Per-task isolated container sandbox with uniform image, unified provider gateway capturing token-level cost on every LLM call; 30-minute wall-clock cap. Paired-n denominators: pairwise n=80 (SC-ON vs SC-OFF) and n=78 (SC-ON vs OpenCode). Headline magnitudes (mean of seed means): resolve 50.4/41.9/45.3%, acc@5 View B 84.5/44.3/75.3%, $/solved $2.30/$2.84/$2.92, $/cell $1.15/$1.19/$1.32, turns 28.3/36.2/36.0, tokens 10.1k/11.1k/14.0k, wall-clock 4.5/5.5/5.4 min. Statistics: mean of seed means with across-seed SD; paired Wilcoxon signed-rank (two-sided, normal approximation) on per-instance pass@1.
facts.limitations: Single-model scope only (Claude Opus 4.7) is an explicitly acknowledged limitation; the control trade is intentional. Cross-harness comparison vs OpenCode on resolve (p=0.087) and View B acc@5 (p=0.080) is marginal and not at conventional significance; the within-harness ablation is the cleaner read. Closed-source harnesses (Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf) are out of scope by design. Language coverage excludes JavaScript and TypeScript. Sandbox backend configs and image spec are not public (per-cell patches, traces, prompts, sandbox image references held back due to licensed repo source and internal harness config). The study addresses solution-leakage and in-benchmark memorization via detect-and-exclude hardening but does NOT address the phrasing-ecological-validity threat (Garg et al. report >50% capability overestimation for some models). The per-language and per-file-count slices (Section 6.3) are explicitly exploratory with n=18-46 and no significance claims.
facts.project_relevance: Directly on-topic for the agent-acceleration card's central question of whether a code knowledge graph / structural codebase index reduces real-task repeated Read/Grep and improves end-to-end resolve and cost. It is one of the cleanest causal reads available: model, prompts, sandbox, scorer and seeds are held identical and only the two engine tools are toggled. The absolute magnitudes now confirm a large tool-call reduction: mean turns drop from 36.2 to 28.3 (-8.3, p<0.0001) and mean tokens from 11.1k to 10.1k (-1.6k, p=0.027) with per-cell cost statistically null ($1.15 vs $1.19, p=0.73), yielding a lower $/solved ($2.30 vs $2.84). The structural index pays off most where changes span 3+ files (+46.4pp acc@5), matching the project's 'reduce repeated Read/Grep in multi-file changes' goal. It releases the per-cell ledger, leak-audit script and localization extractor, enabling replication.

brief_item.mechanism: 完全二部图核心加正交双划分使路径多样性指数恒为1，对任意流量矩阵可证均衡故对Braess免疫。
brief_item.result: 千卡GLM-5.1集群零改动迁移后网络成本降33%，吞吐升15%，P99 TTFT降40.6%。
brief_item.boundary: 恢复依赖中心化控制器为毫秒级，收益来自单集群单模型族未做因子分解。

facts.title: Fewer Paths, Better Performance: Understanding the ZCube Topology through Braess's Paradox
facts.event_hint: Analyzes the ZCube datacenter topology (removes the Spine layer, eliminates path multiplicity) via Braess's paradox, and reports first public production inference evidence: a 1000-GPU GLM-5.1 coding-inference cluster migrated from rail-optimized Fat-Tree (ROFT) to ZCube with zero GPU/software/model-config change.
facts.problem: Datacenter networks follow a multipath doctrine (provision many paths, hash flows via ECMP, let redundancy absorb imbalance). ZCube violates it by removing the Spine layer and eliminating path multiplicity, yet reports better performance for both LLM training and inference. The paper asks why fewer paths can help, and frames the answer through Braess's paradox: under congestion-oblivious routing over competing paths, adding paths can hurt (Braess) and removing paths can help (ZCube). For structured LLM traffic (Prefill-to-Decode KV cache transfers that are asymmetric and physically clustered), ECMP hashing produces persistent, pattern-correlated link hotspots that rehashing does not remove.
facts.mechanism: ZCube uses a complete bipartite K_{m,m} core with an orthogonal dual partition (odd/even switch groups) that provably balances load for arbitrary traffic matrices; its Path Diversity Index is PDI=1 by construction, making it provably immune to Braess's paradox (PDI>=2 is a necessary condition for Braess vulnerability, and Fat-Tree has PDI=m). The authors bound greedy routing's Price of Anarchy at 4/3 of optimal for affine latencies while static ECMP admits unbounded worst-case imbalance. AllReduce (training) and KV-cache transfers (disaggregated inference) fall out as two corollaries of the load-spreading theorem. The price of immunity is failover: Fat-Tree recovers locally in microseconds via hash recomputation, while ZCube recovers via a centralized controller on a millisecond scale (core-link fault domain is 1/m^2 of pairs; for n=16384, k=128, m=128 that is 0.006% of pairs), with path length rising from 2 to 4 hops after a detour. The trade favors LLM serving because failures are rare (hardware annual failure <1%, so ZCube runs at optimum >99% of the time) while Fat-Tree pays its 'Braess tax' every day.

evidence.claim: Production measurement on a 1000-GPU cluster serving GLM-5.1 coding inference, migrated from rail-optimized Fat-Tree (ROFT) to ZCube with no GPU/software/model-config change (topology is the only variable): network cost (switches + optical modules) fell 33%, average GPU inference throughput rose 15%, and P99 TTFT fell 40.6%.
evidence.value: -33% network cost; +15% GPU throughput; -40.6% P99 TTFT
evidence.condition: 1000-GPU GLM-5.1 coding inference cluster, disaggregated Prefill/Decode, zero-change migration, stable for several weeks at time of writing
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 2 (Introduction); PDF Page 4 (Table 2, Section 3.2 Production Evidence)

evidence.claim: The authors explicitly treat the throughput/latency gain as a hypothesis rather than a foregone conclusion: 'the throughput and latency gains exceed what the bandwidth change alone predicts', and attribute them to topology via the zero-change migration rather than a full decomposition of contributing factors (stated as a limitation).
evidence.value: gains exceed bandwidth-change prediction; attribution is by zero-change migration, not factor decomposition
evidence.condition: GLM-5.1 coding inference cluster
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 4 (Section 3.2); PDF Page 10 (Limitations, fourth item)

evidence.claim: PDI characterization: a Braess subgraph requires at least two competing routes, so PDI>=2 is necessary for Braess vulnerability. Fat-Tree has PDI=m (m Spine paths); ZCube has PDI=1 by construction, which is the structural basis of its immunity.
evidence.value: ZCube PDI=1; Fat-Tree PDI=m
evidence.condition: topological Path Diversity Index definition
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 4 (Section defining PDI, Eq. 2)

evidence.claim: Simulated link-load imbalance (max/mean, 1.0=perfect balance) on n=128 GPUs, k=16/switch, m=8/group, 500 ECMP hash seeds for ROFT: under uniform AllReduce ROFT+ECMP pays residual imbalance 1.14 vs ZCube 1.00; under clustered 25/75 Prefill-to-Decode ROFT reaches 4.50 while ZCube stays 1.33 (exactly 1.00 on links carrying the pattern's traffic); under 8 adversarial elephant flows both degrade to ~9 (the honest boundary: the theorem disperses structured clusters, not arbitrary point flows).
evidence.value: ROFT 1.14 vs ZCube 1.00 (AllReduce); ROFT 4.50 vs ZCube 1.33 (25/75 PD); both ~9 (elephants)
evidence.condition: simulated n=128, k=16, m=8 fabric; four traffic patterns
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 9 (Section 7.2, Figure 2)

evidence.claim: Failure-recovery trade (Table 3): Fat-Tree+ECMP recovers via distributed hash recomputation in microseconds with unchanged path length; ZCube recovers via a centralized controller in milliseconds with path length rising 2->4 hops, core-link fault domain = 1/m^2 of pairs (0.006% for n=16384,k=128,m=128). The trade favors LLM serving because hardware failure rate is <1%/year so ZCube runs at optimum >99% of the time while Fat-Tree pays its Braess tax continuously.
evidence.value: recovery us (Fat-Tree) vs ms (ZCube); ZCube fault domain 0.006% of pairs; hardware failure <1%/yr
evidence.condition: single core-link / switch / access-link failure analysis
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 8 (Table 3, Section 6.2-6.3)

facts.evaluation_context: Production: a 1000-GPU cluster serving GLM-5.1 coding inference, disaggregated Prefill/Decode (Prefill nodes transfer large KV cache volumes to Decode nodes), migrated from rail-optimized Fat-Tree (ROFT) to ZCube with topology as the only variable (no GPU, software-stack, or model-serving-config change), stable for several weeks. Baseline: ROFT pre-migration. Metrics: switches+optical-module cost, average GPU inference throughput, P99 TTFT. Simulation: n=128 GPUs, k=16 GPUs/switch, m=8 switches/group, ROFT models ECMP over 500 random hash seeds, ZCube computes core link loads deterministically; four traffic patterns (uniform AllReduce, 25/75 and 50/50 clustered Prefill-to-Decode, 8 random elephant flows). Theory: Price of Anarchy bounded at 4/3 for greedy routing on affine latencies (Roughgarden-Tardos); PDI-based Braess-vulnerability characterization.
facts.limitations: Four explicitly stated limits: (1) the complete bipartite K_{m,m} core requires switch radix to grow with m, so very large clusters need hierarchical extensions; (2) the K_{m,m} core has substantial wiring complexity, handled with automated layout/validation tooling; (3) failure recovery depends on a centralized controller, a single point of operational risk; (4) production evidence comes from one cluster serving one model family, and gains are attributed to topology through the zero-change migration rather than a full decomposition of contributing factors. The throughput/latency gains exceed what bandwidth change alone predicts and are treated as a hypothesis validated by analysis, not a foregone conclusion. Simulation n=128 is much smaller than the 1000-GPU (or 16384-GPU theoretical) deployment. Per-link utilization and TTFT distributions before/after migration are stated to be 'in preparation for a future revision' (not in the visible evidence). The failure-recovery comparison is qualitative (microseconds vs milliseconds) without absolute measured values.
facts.project_relevance: Directly relevant to the TPN card's question of whether network-side mechanisms reduce KV-cache cross-node transfer congestion and improve end-to-end TTFT/throughput. The production result (-40.6% P99 TTFT, +15% throughput) is attributed precisely to structural congestion removal on the Prefill-to-Decode KV-cache transfer path: on ROFT, contiguous Prefill blocks overload a small set of Leaf uplinks (pattern-correlated hotspots that rehashing does not remove), while ZCube's orthogonal dual partition provably balances arbitrary traffic matrices including the asymmetric clustered KV transfer pattern. This is a concrete answer to the card's question of what network-side topology matching adds over GPU/memory-side scheduling. Caveats for project use: the gain is from one cluster/one model family with attribution by zero-change migration rather than factor decomposition, and finer per-link/TTFT telemetry is not yet public.

evidence_gaps.question: What are the absolute P99 TTFT (ms), GPU throughput (tokens/s or req/s), and per-link utilization numbers behind the -40.6%/+15%/-33% production ratios, and the absolute failure-recovery latencies (us vs ms) behind Table 3?

brief_item.title: Deep Agentic搜索实证：子Agent委托在仓库级代码QA上不如向量检索
brief_item.core_conclusion: 主流Deep Agentic搜索在仓库级代码QA上反而不如向量索引检索，规划到子Agent的交接本身成了最大失败来源。
brief_item.mechanism: 对比ReAct加向量索引与规划器委托隔离子Agent两套架构，工具空间与编排差异作为范式固有变量。
brief_item.result: SWE-QA上语义检索Pass率65.2%对46.2%，每个正确答案成本不足对方一半。
brief_item.boundary: 仅限可索引Python仓库的只读QA，未覆盖写补丁任务。
brief_item.project_relevance: 可索引的只读仓库问题应优先用语义检索，把子Agent探索留给真正难写的场景。

facts.title: Deep Agentic Search for Repository-Level Code Question Answering: An Empirical Study
facts.event_hint: Empirical comparison of Semantic search (vector index + ReAct) vs Deep Agentic search (grep-search by isolated subagent) for repository-level code QA on SWE-QA across four LLMs; finds Semantic more accurate and cheaper, with a large failure share of Deep Agentic at the planner->subagent hand-off.
facts.problem: Code agents spend much of their effort locating the right code inside a repository, and two paradigms dominate current practice: Semantic search (retrieve code blocks from a pre-built vector index) and Deep Agentic search (a planning agent delegates exploration to a separate subagent working in an isolated context window, returning only a condensed result, to protect the main agent from context pollution/context rot). Recent code agents (Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity) have quickly adopted Deep Agentic search as 'good context engineering practice', but there was little empirical evidence on whether it actually produces better answers than indexed retrieval for repository-level code QA.
facts.mechanism: Two agent architectures compared on the SWE-QA benchmark (Peng et al., 2026a; open-ended What/Why/Where/How questions over whole Python repositories, 15 repos x 48 questions = 720 questions per condition; 12 repos drawn from SWE-bench and 3 from SWE-bench-Live). Semantic: a ReAct agent (LangChain SWE-QA Agent harness) restricted to three tools (repository structure lookup, retrieval over a vector index built once per repository by chunking and embedding files, and a file reader), with no shell/filesystem-write/planning tools. Deep Agentic: a Deep Agent (LangChain Deep Agents framework harness with default toolset including planning, a virtual filesystem, and sub-agent delegation), in which a planning orchestrator delegates exploration to an isolated sub-agent that returns a condensed result; orchestrator and sub-agent use the same model. Each question answered in a fresh conversation thread, only the targeted repository available, all execution traces recorded. Tool-space and orchestration differences are treated as constitutive of the paradigms (a paradigm-bundle comparison, not a single-factor ablation). Grading: LLM judge Claude Sonnet 4.6 (different provider/family from every answering model), five dimensions combined to a 0-100 score with three-class verdict (Pass >=70, Partial 50-69, Fail <50). Three RQs plus a six-mechanism/five-symptom failure taxonomy (two-author inter-rater Cohen's kappa 0.86 symptom / 0.78 mechanism).

evidence.claim: On SWE-QA (720 questions per condition, 15 Python repos), Semantic search answered 65.2% of questions correctly vs 46.2% for Deep Agentic search (pooled headline), and Semantic produced each correct answer at less than half the cost of Deep Agentic.
evidence.value: 65.2% vs 46.2% Pass; Semantic <half the $/correct of Deep Agentic
evidence.condition: SWE-QA repository-level code QA, 720 questions/condition, 15 Python repos, four LLMs (Gemini 2.5 Flash, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Gemini 3 Flash, Qwen3-235B), LLM judge Claude Sonnet 4.6 validated vs human panel
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 1 (Abstract); PDF Page 15 (Table 3 master comparison)

evidence.claim: Per-model Pass-rate advantage for Semantic over Deep Agentic: +5.6pp (Gemini 2.5 Flash), +10.0pp (Gemini 2.5 Pro), +10.6pp (Qwen3-235B) and +49.6pp (Gemini 3 Flash); all four McNemar and all four Wilcoxon tests remained significant after FDR correction. Cliff's delta on score ~0.14 for the two Gemini 2.5 models, ~0.24 for Qwen3-235B, ~0.76 for Gemini 3 Flash.
evidence.value: +5.6 / +10.0 / +10.6 / +49.6 pp Semantic advantage; all FDR-significant
evidence.condition: paired within-model comparison, SWE-QA, four LLMs, McNemar + Wilcoxon with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR, bootstrap CIs, Cliff's delta
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 15 (Table 4, Fig. 7 narrative)

evidence.claim: Deep Agentic search did not remove failures but introduced a new failure class: the single largest share of its failures, 41.8%, occurred at the planner-to-sub-agent hand-off (coordination breakdown), which is structurally impossible for the flat Semantic agent; the association between architecture and failure mechanism is very strong (chi-square 508.8 on 5 df, Cramer's V 0.56; excluding the Deep-only mechanism, chi-square 147.2 on 4 df, Cramer's V 0.35).
evidence.value: 41.8% of Deep failures at hand-off; chi-square 508.8 df5 V=0.56 (147.2 df4 V=0.35 excluding Deep-only)
evidence.condition: failure taxonomy coded from recorded traces, SWE-QA, four LLMs
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 26 (Section 6.3 Failure distributions, Figure 19)

evidence.claim: Memorization/leakage check (Section 8 External validity): splitting the 15 repos by provenance (12 SWE-bench vs 3 SWE-bench-Live), Semantic led on both subsets for every model, and the pooled advantage was somewhat larger on the three later SWE-bench-Live repos (15.9 vs 12.7 points), the opposite of what an advantage driven by memorization would predict; treated as a descriptive check, not a test.
evidence.value: Semantic leads both subsets; pooled advantage 15.9pp (SWE-bench-Live) vs 12.7pp (SWE-bench), opposite to memorization prediction
evidence.condition: provenance split of SWE-QA repos, paired within-model
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 32 (Section 8 External validity)

evidence.claim: Judge validity: on a stratified sample of 800 answers (100 per condition), human-majority vs LLM-judge agreement was Cohen's kappa 0.74 (84.0% exact agreement) on the categorical verdict and Pearson r=0.83 / Spearman rho=0.81 / MAD 5.2 score points on the harmonized 0-100 score; human panel internal Fleiss' kappa 0.81; judge is a different provider/family from every answering model.
evidence.value: human vs judge kappa 0.74 (84.0%); Pearson r=0.83; MAD 5.2; panel Fleiss' kappa 0.81
evidence.condition: stratified 800-answer sample, 100 per condition, three-class verdict + harmonized 0-100 score
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 15 (Table 2 Judge validity)

facts.evaluation_context: Benchmark: SWE-QA (Peng et al., 2026a), repository-level code QA over 15 Python repositories (12 from SWE-bench + 3 from SWE-bench-Live), 48 questions each = 720 questions/condition, four interrogative categories (What/Why/Where/How) in roughly equal proportion; each question in a fresh thread with only the targeted repository available. Two architectures: ReAct + Semantic search (vector index over chunked files, three tools) vs Deep Agent + Deep Agentic search (planner + isolated sub-agent, default Deep Agents toolset; orchestrator and sub-agent use the same model). Four LLMs: Gemini 2.5 Flash (0.30/2.50 $/M in/out), Gemini 2.5 Pro (1.25/10.00), Gemini 3 Flash (0.50/3.00), Qwen3-235B (0.22/0.88); reasoning tokens billed at output rate. Grading: LLM judge Claude Sonnet 4.6 (different provider/family from all answering models), five dimensions -> 0-100 score, Pass>=70/Partial 50-69/Fail<50, validated vs independent three-rater human panel on 800 stratified answers. Failure taxonomy: six mechanisms/five symptoms, two-author inter-rater kappa 0.86/0.78.
facts.limitations: The two agent action spaces are intentionally not identical (tool and orchestration differences co-vary by design; the authors read this as a paradigm-bundle comparison, not a single-factor ablation, and did not run sensitivity across alternative deep-agent harnesses). SWE-QA targets read-only repository-level code QA over Python repositories that can be pre-indexed; the authors explicitly state in External Validity that findings may NOT transfer to other benchmarks, other models, or other (non-Python) languages, and they did not test write/patch (SWE-bench-style) tasks — Section 7 notes tasks that 'write and execute code' are precisely where heavier deep-agent orchestration may be justified. The repos are drawn from SWE-bench/SWE-bench-Live but the task is QA, not patching. The headline 65.2% vs 46.2% pools across four models of very different capability (Gemini 3 Flash alone shows a 49.6pp gap while the Gemini 2.5 pair shows ~5.6-10pp), so the pooled number overstates the typical gap. Cost columns exclude some token categories from displayed token counts (reasoning tokens billed but reported separately), so $/q is not derivable from shown token columns. The LLM judge has MAD 5.2 score points and lower agreement on Deep conditions. Latency was heavy-tailed and environment-sensitive, so no conclusion is based on it.
facts.project_relevance: Highly relevant and contrarian for the agent-acceleration card: it directly tests the now-popular Deep Agentic / grep-by-subagent design (adopted by Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity) against indexed Semantic retrieval on a real repo-QA benchmark and finds Semantic retrieval both more accurate and roughly half the cost per correct answer, with the Deep design introducing a new silent failure mode (41.8% of its failures at the planner->subagent hand-off, often ending in fluent confident wrong answers). Actionable for the project: for read-only repo questions that can be indexed, retrieval is the stronger and cheaper default, and the context-pollution protection of sub-agent delegation is not free; a hybrid that keeps a cheap semantic index and reserves delegated exploration for genuinely hard cases is suggested (future work). Important scope caveat (now explicit): the result is for QA over indexable Python repos only; the authors flag that write/patch tasks, non-Python repos, and non-indexable environments are where deep agents may be justified, so this complements rather than contradicts papers showing structural indices helping patch resolve.

evidence_gaps.question: Do the accuracy/cost conclusions hold for write/patch (SWE-bench-style) tasks and for non-Python repositories, or only for read-only Python repo QA?
